transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2027-06-30
- Start: 15:00 UTC
- Duration: ~49 minutes
- Attendees: Liam Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Jordan Wells (Redwood SE); Oliver Reed (CTO), Sana Kapoor (Lead ML Eng), Marcus Lim (SRE), Aisha Rahman (PM)

Summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect):
Redwood walked through integration options, SDKs, and recommended patterns for Cypress. Customer focused on integrating with LangChain/LlamaIndex, whether to put Redwood behind their gateway/proxy, rate limiting behavior under burst, and how to wire observability hooks (trace ids, token-level cost breakdown). Security questions around VPC/private and KMS were raised; Redwood to share examples and pricing.

Transcript:
[00:00] Liam: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros — i'm liam from redwood, joining me is priya and jordan. how's everyone doing?
[00:07] Oliver: good, thanks. oliver here, cto at cypress. we've got sana, marcus, and aisha on the line.
[00:12] Sana: hi all.
[00:13] Marcus: hey.
[00:15] Liam: great. goal for today is to understand your integration surface — sdk usage, connectors like langchain or llama index, whether you want redwood behind your proxy, rate limits, and what observability you need. we'll try to be concrete.
[00:26] Aisha: yep, that's perfect. we've been experimenting with a mix of open models and hosted apis, and want to figure out which deployment mode makes sense: hosted, dedicated, or private.
[00:35] Priya: quick clarifying question — what are your primary workloads? routing support conversations + developer code-assist inside product?
[00:40] Oliver: both. routing first — classify + route incoming tickets, enrich with embeddings to find past threads. second is code-assist for our internal developer tooling, lower latency needs.
[00:50] Sana: for embeddings we use a small batch async pipeline, but for code-assist it's interactive so latency matters — sub 200ms token response ideally.
[00:58] Jordan: ok makes sense. on sdk side our clients typically integrate via our HTTP SDK (rest + streaming) or via our python sdk — we have examples for langchain and llamaindex. do you have an existing langchain flow?
[01:08] Oliver: we do. we've got a langchain pipeline for retrieval augmented generation and a llamaindex wrapper in python. main ask: how much work to swap the model endpoint to redwood and keep our existing chains?
[01:18] Priya: typically it's small — we provide a LangChain LLM wrapper and an embeddings client. in python it's often 5-10 lines: change the llm/embeddings provider to redwood client, swap endpoint key, and adjust polling for streaming if you're using that. we'll share code snippets.
[01:30] Sana: ok good. what about LlamaIndex specifically? we rely on node and python clients for different services.
[01:36] Priya: we have both. for LlamaIndex we provide direct call patterns and examples for prompt templates, and ways to attach our streaming chunks to LlamaIndex callbacks. again will share examples in the repo.
[01:45] Marcus: question on proxies — our infra policy requires all outbound AI calls go through a centralized gateway/proxy for auditing and DLP. can redwood sit behind a customer proxy? we also might want to do IP whitelisting.
[01:57] Liam: yes — supported. hosted can be used with an egress proxy: your agents call your gateway which then calls redwood's public api. we also support setting up allowlisted IPs and customer-specific ingress rules. for dedicated/private we can deploy inside your vpc or provide private endpoints so no public egress is needed.
[02:14] Marcus: if we proxy, do we lose streaming? we rely on streaming for the UI.
[02:19] Priya: streaming works through proxies; you'll want to ensure the proxy preserves chunked transfers / SSE. sometimes proxies buffer — that's a config on your gateway. we include a small checklist for nginx/envoy settings.
[02:31] Marcus: cool. and auth? we use short-lived tokens and rotate via k8s service accounts.
[02:36] Jordan: we support header-based api keys and oauth flows; for private deployments we integrate with your own KMS for signing tokens. we also have an option for mTLS on dedicated/private to authenticate at the connection layer.
[02:47] Sana: about quotas and rate limits — if our support routing spikes, how are bursts handled? we don't want throttling to drop messages.
[02:55] Liam: on hosted we enforce per-account rate limits but support burst tokens and tiered quotas; we can set soft limits with queueing or hard limits with 429s. dedicated gives you reserved GPU capacity so you're insulated from multi-tenant bursts and you can configure autoscale policies and burst buckets. for critical paths we recommend dedicated or a hybrid fallback policy where routed low-priority requests go to a cheaper model.
[03:17] Aisha: is there SLA for latency on dedicated?
[03:20] Liam: yes — dedicated includes latency SLOs backed in the contract; exact numbers depend on model size and instance type. we'll put sample numbers in the pricing doc.
[03:28] Oliver: on observability — we need traceability back to app request ids and per-token cost breakdown for chargeback. how does redwood expose that?
[03:36] Priya: we emit structured request-level logs with request_id propagation. you can pass your trace id in headers; it surfaces in logs and our console. token-level breakdown and cost attribution is available in the console and via our billing APIs as CSV/JSON exports. we also provide tracing hooks: OpenTelemetry-compatible spans for long-running requests and sampling options.
[03:58] Sana: do you have SDK hooks for attaching our own metadata to turns so we can join traces?
[04:03] Priya: yes, metadata headers and a 'client_meta' field you can send per call that ends up in logs/console. we'll include examples.
[04:11] Marcus: regarding private deployment — if we go private on-premises, how do kernel optimizations and quantization get handled? we run A100/ H100 clusters.
[04:21] Jordan: our runtime supports multiple quantization profiles and auto kernel selection; in private installs we ship the runtime and a small control plane that your team manages. we can work with your hardware team to ensure NVidia drivers and CUDA/ROCm configs. for H100 we'll recommend specific kernel builds and we'll run a short compatibility test.
[04:38] Marcus: any concerns about our air-gapped constraints? we can't allow outbound reachability initially.
[04:44] Liam: for air-gapped we offer an on-prem package where the data plane runs fully standalone; control plane can be deployed in your environment depending on needs. there are licensing/ops implications but it's doable.
[04:55] Sana: latency target — for interactive code-assist we need cold-start under 200ms for token generation, average. is that realistic on dedicated?
[05:03] Jordan: depends on model and batch sizing. with dedicated and optimized kernels we can get into margins you described for smaller models; for larger Llama2-like models you'll need 1-2 tokens latency higher. we can bench this in a POC with your typical prompt lengths.
[05:18] Aisha: about cost — what's the typical unit economics when switching from open host to dedicated? we currently pay per-token on public APIs.
[05:24] Liam: hosted per-token is straightforward; dedicated moves you to reserved capacity pricing with an effective lower per-token cost but requires committed spend. Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization and batching to reduce unit cost; we'll include sample TCO tables.
[05:36] Oliver: good. one more thing — data retention and audit logs. we need to ensure we can disable retention for PII.
[05:43] Priya: we offer retention controls per-tenant and per-route. in dedicated/private you control retention entirely. hosted has configurable retention windows and audit logs export.
[05:52] Marcus: from infra side, network egress and firewall rules — what ports and endpoints should we allow for hosted?
[05:59] Jordan: primarily HTTPS to api.redwood.com endpoints; we'll provide a CIDR allowlist for static ranges if you want to restrict egress. if using streaming you need to allow chunked responses on port 443.
[06:12] Sana: anything special for LangChain connectors for retries/backoff? we have transient 503s occasionally.
[06:18] Priya: we recommend exponential backoff with jitter; our python sdk has a built-in retry policy configurable per route and per error code. for critical interactive flows, use a circuit breaker on the client side and fallback model routes.
[06:30] Oliver: ok that helps. on the SDK level — will we need to refactor our LangChain prompts or is it plug-and-play?
[06:36] Priya: usually plug-and-play. small prompt templating differences may exist if you use model-specific system messages. otherwise it's just changing the provider. we'll put a migration checklist in the repo.
[06:46] Aisha: timeline — we're targeting a POC within 2-3 weeks.
[06:49] Liam: sounds doable. propose: we share examples + pricing + network stencil this week, you confirm success criteria, and we kick off POC next week.
[06:58] Sana: yes. can you include a LangChain chat example with streaming in node? that's our primary LangChain runtime.
[07:05] Priya: will do.
[07:07] (brief crosstalk)
[07:14] Oliver: thanks everyone — useful call.
[07:16] Liam: recap: priya will send SDK + LangChain/LlamaIndex examples; liam will send pricing + sample SLOs; marcus to send network/firewall; cypress to confirm POC success criteria. schedule follow-up poc scoping next week.
[07:30] End of recording.
